tracks.title: You already built your tools
tracks.text: Lesson three point one — imports. A sub-lesson, under toolkit. The parent lesson sold you the unit — a real program in a sandbox, wrapped in a manual — and ended on convert one tool you love. This page is how. [curious] Because here's the thing. Your capabilities don't sit in a vacuum waiting to be written. They already exist… in other people's formats. A folder of Claude skills. An mcp dot json three projects depend on. An OpenAPI spec. An npm CLI. The price nobody admits to is rewriting all of it in the new shape — and that price is exactly why most new formats are born dead. Nobody pays it. So import isn't a clever converter. It's an honest ramp… convert what's convertible, do the real work where it can, and where it genuinely can't… leave instructions instead of a shrug. Convert… don't rewrite.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. Import is the ecosystem's intake ramp. It detects a source's shape… translates its docs to org… scaffolds a real toolkit — manifest, skills, carried scripts — and writes the conversion plan it can't finish for you. The spec states the ethic without hedging. Parse what's parseable… do the work… and leave a manual. Never a shrug. And that last clause is the whole point. An import that can't fully convert your tool does not fail, and does not pretend. [curious] It produces a finished toolkit plan — written in the same grammar agents already execute — and hands you the rest as a checklist. Parse-only, local-only, at this stage. Nothing is built. Nothing runs. Nothing is trusted yet. And a guidance-only toolkit — pure manual, no code — is a valid landing… not a consolation prize.

tracks.title: Nine shapes, one sniff
tracks.text: Nine shapes, one sniff. Detection is not AI and not magic — it's literal shape-sniffing. Import knows nine source kinds, and each maps to what it becomes. Walk a few. First… a Claude skill, detected by a skill dot md with frontmatter, becomes a main skill plus one reference skill per reference file. Second… a lone markdown file becomes a one-skill toolkit, the doc as its manual. Third… an mcp dot json becomes a skill per server, plus a synthesized launch script. Fourth… an OpenAPI spec — detected by the word openapi appearing in the first four kilobytes, content not extension — becomes a skill per operation. Fifth… an npm CLI, a package dot json with a bin, gets a scope-stripped id and its README as the manual. And the rest — a pip CLI, cursor rules, an agents dot md — each lands somewhere too. [curious] The order of the sniff is the careful part. Identity files win before the generic markdown catch-all — a folder with a skill dot md is a Claude skill, not just a pile of markdown. And a directory always lands somewhere. If nothing else matches… it imports as a plain folder. One honest note — the inline help for the as flag lists only three kinds, but the parser accepts all nine… and its error message is the source of truth.

tracks.title: Three honest stages
tracks.text: Three honest stages. A ramp has stages, and these three are kept distinct so none of them can lie on behalf of another. First… parse and scaffold — detect the shape, translate the docs, write a real toolkit to disk. A manifest, a skills tree, any carried scripts. Second… the dependency audit. And this one runs automatically, at the end of every import. It classifies each carried script against the wasm lanes and writes the findings into the manifest itself — the artifact carries its own audit, not a side report. Third… the fix-up plan. Everything not already sandbox-ready becomes an org checklist with concrete rewrite recipes. Now picture the whole ramp as a graph. On the far left… a source — a skill, an mcp config, an OpenAPI spec, a CLI. An arrow into detect, which sniffs the shape. Then into the per-kind parser, which turns markdown into org and collects scripts. Then into scaffold, which writes the manifest, the skills, the scripts. Then into audit, which auto-runs. And it all flows into one box — the manifest dot org, carrying its findings and its fix-up plan. There's one more arrow, and it's dotted — labeled still ahead — pointing at push, build, verify. [curious] That dotted edge is the honest part of the picture. An import produces an artifact… not a running tool. Imported is not runnable… is not trusted. And if the audit fails to run at all, the import still succeeds — it degrades to a quiet audit-skipped note rather than throwing the conversion away. The manual always lands.

tracks.title: The honest ninety percent
tracks.text: The honest ninety percent. A depth rung — skippable, but it's where the word honest earns its keep. The doc translator is mechanical and deterministic. No model… no inference. It walks the markdown and rewrites the constructs it knows, line by line. A hash heading becomes a star heading, same depth. A triple-backtick code fence becomes begin-source, end-source. A markdown link — text in brackets, url in parens — flips to org's order, url first, then text. Double-star bold becomes single-star bold. And inline backtick code becomes equals-wrapped code. [curious] The thesis is one comment in the source — what it can't translate, it passes through… because org tolerates it. Lists, tables, images — untouched, and they still read, because org is a superset that doesn't choke on stray markdown. That's why ninety percent is the right number to promise and a hundred is the wrong one. The translator never guesses… so it never mangles. Ten percent rides through as-is. That's the deal, stated plainly.

tracks.title: What lands on disk
tracks.text: What lands on disk. A scaffold is a real toolkit, not a sketch. The manifest carries a fixed set of keys that mark its provenance — most importantly, status imported, and imported-from kind and source — so the artifact always remembers where it came from. And it refuses to overwrite an existing directory. Already exists… full stop. Walk the Claude skill round trip. The input — a directory with a skill dot md, a reference doc, and a shell script. The skill's frontmatter says name, demo-skill… description, does demo things. One command — wbx toolkit import my-skill. And the output reads back like this. Imported claude-skill into demo-skill-toolkit. A manifest dot org… the toolkit surface. A skills folder… two skills. A scripts folder… one carried, unaudited, see the TODO. Then a next line — review the manifest, then verify. And below that, the audit already ran — audited one script, one ready, zero convertible, zero blocked. Run dot sh… ready… it's shell. Findings written into the manifest. [excited] And the manifest itself carries the trust posture in its own body, verbatim — anything under scripts is carried verbatim and NOT yet trusted to run in the sandbox. For an all-shell skill like this, the fix-up section reads… nothing to fix, every script is sandbox-ready. The fence came across as begin-source bash. The link flipped to org order. Every claim in that walkthrough is a line in the test suite.

tracks.title: Manufacturing evidence
tracks.text: Manufacturing evidence. A depth rung — and the cleverest mechanic in the whole verb. For two kinds, import synthesizes a script that doesn't exist in the source… specifically so the audit has something honest to judge. The system manufactures the evidence for its own honesty pass. [curious] Take an MCP server. Its config never contains a script — it contains a launch command. But the server IS the bin. Running it is the capability. So picture the sequence. The mcp dot json names a server, gh, whose command is npx, dash y, at-x slash server. Import synthesizes scripts slash gh dot sh, holding exactly that — exec npx, dash y, at-x slash server. It hands that real script to the audit. The audit classifies npx — the npm lane exists. And it writes the verdict into the manifest. Gh dot sh… convertible… resolve and bundle at build time. Now the pip CLI uses the same trick toward the opposite verdict. From a pyproject console script, import synthesizes a tiny Python stub holding only the entry-point comment. It exists so the audit can say the true thing — blocked, no python lane today — and hand the rewrite recipe to an agent. The stub is a placeholder for honesty… not a working tool.

tracks.title: Names travel, values don't
tracks.text: Names travel… values don't. An MCP config routinely carries secrets — an API token sitting in an env block. Import documents the env names in the skill and synthesizes the launcher… but the values never leave the source. Look at what lands. The input has a server, gh, with command npx, and an env holding a token whose value is hunter-two. The output… a script, gh dot sh, that just runs exec npx, dash y, at-x slash server — no token in sight. And a skill that says, env, names only, set values engine-side… token. [excited] The string hunter-two appears in zero output files — manifest, skill, and script are all checked, and the test asserts it. The name token is documented, so a human knows what to set. The value stays put. Config values may be secrets… so they're treated as secrets by default. And the same skill is honest about a second limit — MCP tools are enumerated at runtime, not in the config. So the import documents the launcher, not the tool list, and says so. Run the server to list its tools… then write each as its own skill.

tracks.title: Guidance-only is a landing
tracks.text: Guidance-only is a landing. Not every source has code, and the ramp doesn't punish that. A cursor-rules file, a cursor rules directory, an agents dot md, or a bare markdown doc — all import into a toolkit that is pure manual. Skills, and no scripts. The audit, finding nothing to convert, writes the cleanest possible verdict — no carried scripts, guidance-only toolkit, nothing to convert. The test feeds it an agents dot md and asserts the import reports nothing to fix. A guidance-only toolkit is a clean landing… not a failure. [curious] This is the lowest, most stable rung of the ladder the parent lesson named — the manual is the interface. A toolkit that is only a manual is still a real toolkit. Installable… versioned… readable by an agent. Sometimes the most valuable thing you have to convert is know-how… and the ramp carries know-how as a first-class artifact.

tracks.title: The honest limits
tracks.text: Now the honest limits. House rule on these pages — name the edges in the source's own words. First… remote refs aren't wired. A skills dot sh slug, an owner-slash-repo, an http url — none import directly. Instead of half-trying, the error teaches the fix. Clone it locally, then import the folder. Second… YAML OpenAPI isn't parsed. Only JSON specs parse today, and a YAML spec gets a recipe, not a half-parse — convert it first with yq, then import the JSON. Third… MCP tools are runtime-enumerated. Fourth… no python lane today, so a python script audits as blocked. Fifth… translation is ninety percent, not a hundred — lists, tables, images pass through. And sixth… imported is not verified. Push, build, and verify are still ahead. [curious] The blocked case deserves the worked detail, because it's the one most likely to read as a failure when it isn't. From a pyproject exposing a console script called pycli, the manifest gains exactly this. An audit finding — pycli dot py… blocked… python3… no python lane today, rewrite in a covered lane or split the logic. And then a fix-up plan, zero of one done. The agent manual — work each item, check it off, then prove the whole toolkit. Done when push, build, and verify all pass. And with an engine reachable, audit dash dash fix runs that whole chain for you. Below it, the checklist — rewrite in JS for the quickjs lane, keeping the same args in and same stdout out. Or split the logic into org tasks the engine runs natively. Then re-run the audit… pycli must classify ready. [excited] The import didn't fail. It produced the instructions — in the same org grammar agents already execute. The sibling lesson, audits, owns the depth of how those verdicts get decided. This page hands off cleanly at stage two.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Does it use an LLM? No. Detection is filename and content sniffing… translation is mechanical and deterministic… the audit is a static classifier. Run it twice on the same input, get the same scaffold. The intelligence is in the structure, not a model call. My import says blocked — did it fail? No — the plan is the product. Blocked means import couldn't make it sandbox-ready by itself, so it wrote the rewrite recipe instead. An agent works the checklist, and audit dash dash fix proves the result. Can I import straight from skills dot sh or a repo url? Not yet — clone the source locally, then import the folder. What happens to my MCP server's tools list? Tools are enumerated at runtime, so import documents the launcher and tells you to run the server once, then write each tool as a skill. And — will my scripts run after import? [chuckles] Not immediately, and the manifest says so verbatim. Carried scripts are NOT yet trusted to run in the sandbox. Imported is not runnable… is not trusted. Push, build, verify are the gates between a scaffold and a working tool.

tracks.title: Back up to the toolkit
tracks.text: So that's imports. Not magic, and not a converter that lies. An honest ramp — sniff the shape, translate the docs, scaffold a real toolkit… and where it can't finish, leave the plan, never a shrug. [curious] Import is stage one of a longer journey. The way back up is short. The parent lesson, toolkit — lesson three — for the unit you're converting into. And the siblings carry it the rest of the way. Audits, for how ready, convertible, and blocked get decided. Lanes, for why node is ready and python is blocked. And verification, for the real done-test… push… build… verify. Everything import produces is a candidate for those gates — and a manual you can read while it gets there.
